profile.headline: Software Engineer & Software Architect
profile.pitch: I design and build distributed systems that scale, and I lead the teams that run them in production.
summary: Software Engineer and Software Architect with more than 10 years designing and building enterprise systems. As Tech Lead I led 6+ developers, defined the annual roadmap of the applications under my ownership and documented the architecture of more than 10 micro-applications; I take initiatives end to end, from requirements and system design to production monitoring.

My core is .NET/C# and Angular on Azure, with microservices and event-driven architectures (Kafka, RabbitMQ, Azure Service Bus, gRPC), plus recent work with Java and Spring Boot at Mercado Libre. I care about observability, CI/CD and quality gates, and about helping the engineers around me grow through mentoring and code reviews.
M.Sc. in Computer Software Engineering, currently preparing the Azure Solutions Architect Expert (AZ-305) certification. Native Spanish, professional English (B2).

senior.title: Senior Software Engineer
achievements: Developed and evolved Java/Spring Boot microservices that match seller listings with products on the marketplace storefront.
Led the productization project end to end, from requirements to production monitoring, operating a pipeline with peaks of 60,000 productization requests per day, all processed without failures.

Built the results-measurement layer for this asynchronous process (Python scripts, BigQuery and a Looker Studio dashboard refreshed 3 times a day), making visible which requests ended unproductized because of internal and cross-team validations, where there was no visibility before.
Escalated findings to the owning teams to pinpoint failure points and improvement opportunities.
Worked with queues and streaming (Fury) in a distributed, event-driven microservices architecture; integrated NoSQL sources into read-only BigQuery tables.
Monitored production with Datadog and Grafana: built dashboards and analyzed metrics and logs.
Took part in the 24/7 on-call rotation: investigated production incidents, applied temporary mitigations while finding the real problem, and delivered root-cause fixes.
Guided and reviewed the work of less senior engineers (features, debugging, optimization, pull requests) and was onboarding buddy for a new teammate.

Supported teammates with code reviews and led the team when my manager was absent.

microservicesDemo.title: Microservices.Demo — insurance platform
microservicesDemo.context: An insurance platform where authentication, product catalog, pricing, policies and reports evolve and scale independently. The goal was to show, end to end, the building blocks a real microservices platform needs: a single entry point, service discovery, centralized configuration, asynchronous messaging and observability.

interactions.i1: calls every API through the gateway with a JWT
interactions.i2: routes requests to the services found in the registry
interactions.i3: calculates the price of a policy
interactions.i5: composes reports from products and policies
interactions.i6: loads routes and settings at startup
interactions.i8: send structured logs, APM data and traces

d1.decision: Database per service, each with the engine that fits it (MongoDB, SQL Server, PostgreSQL with Marten).
d1.tradeOff: Services own and evolve their data independently, but cross-service views must be composed over the network (Report service).

d2.decision: A single entry point: an Ocelot API Gateway that validates the JWT and routes to the services.
d2.tradeOff: Security and routing policy live in one place, at the cost of an extra hop and a component that must stay highly available.

d3.decision: Eureka service discovery plus Spring Cloud Config, with routes and settings in a separate Git repository.
d3.tradeOff: Configuration changes without rebuilding images, but every service depends on Config Server at startup (fail fast).

d4.decision: Asynchronous events over RabbitMQ when policies change.
d4.tradeOff: Producers and consumers are decoupled and can scale apart, accepting eventual consistency between them.

d5.decision: Observability from day one: ELK for logs, APM Server for metrics and Jaeger for distributed traces.
d5.tradeOff: A request can be followed across services, at the price of a heavier infrastructure footprint.

employeeAttendanceControl.title: EmployeeAttendanceControl — attendance microservices
employeeAttendanceControl.context: A system to manage employees, their user accounts and an auditable attendance history. Each concern has different access patterns and consistency needs, so each service owns its data and they collaborate through events.

interactions.i1: sends every request with a JWT
interactions.i6: creates the user account of every new employee
interactions.i7: appends each attendance change to the history
interactions.i8: reads the history before updating the current state

d1.decision: The gateway checks the JWT and the admin role, and every service validates the token again.
d1.tradeOff: Defense in depth: a service is never exposed without checks, at the cost of duplicated validation.

d2.decision: Employee creation and attendance changes propagate as events over durable RabbitMQ queues.
d2.tradeOff: Services stay loosely coupled and resilient to temporary outages, accepting eventual consistency.

d3.decision: Storage chosen per access pattern: Cassandra for users, SQL Server with Dapper for current state, MongoDB for an append-only history.
d3.tradeOff: Each store fits its workload, but there are three engines to operate and back up.

d4.decision: Clean Architecture layers with CQRS (MediatR) inside every service.
d4.tradeOff: Business rules are isolated and easy to test, at the cost of more files and ceremony.

d5.decision: Central package management and a test that keeps both gateway route catalogs in sync.
d5.tradeOff: Versions and routes never drift, at the cost of a stricter workflow for every change.

eCommerceMajestic.title: E-Commerce Majestic — Go + Angular on AWS
eCommerceMajestic.context: An online store with three roles (admin, seller, shopper), catalog, shopping cart and an AI chatbot. The priority was to deliver a complete product quickly and deploy it to the cloud with containers, keeping the design simple to operate.

interactions.i1: calls the API with a JWT
interactions.i2: forwards traffic to the API containers
interactions.i3: users, roles, categories, products and carts
interactions.i5: runs and scales the front-end and back-end containers

d1.decision: A modular Go REST API (gorilla/mux, GORM) instead of microservices.
d1.tradeOff: Simple to build, test and deploy, but the whole back end scales as one unit.

d2.decision: MySQL for transactional data and MongoDB for the chat history.
d2.tradeOff: Each kind of data uses the model that fits it, with two stores to operate.

d3.decision: Role-based JWT middleware declared on every route (admin, seller, shopper).
d3.tradeOff: Access rules are explicit and easy to audit, at the cost of some repetition.

d4.decision: Containers on AWS: images in ECR, services in ECS behind one Application Load Balancer per tier, MySQL on RDS.
d4.tradeOff: Managed scaling and availability, with more cloud configuration and cost to manage.

d5.decision: The chatbot calls the LLM provider directly from the web app.
d5.tradeOff: Fastest way to prototype, but it exposes the API key; the next step is to proxy those calls through the back end.
